payload.alternatives: Keeping the decisions only in local planning notes: the product would still have no real use of its own. A separate repository for them: the decisions would not travel with the code, and no visitor would see them.
payload.rationale: The product governs its own development where anyone who reads the repository can see it: the decisions behind mnema are recorded, signed and verified with mnema. The rule of August 2026 against a record here answered probes that had written into it; every probe now runs in a throwaway home and a worktree, never in this clone.
payload.title: Keep this repository's own mnema record, committed with it

fields.note: Accepted by the maintainer on 14 October 2026. The .gitignore line that keeps .mnema/ out of the repository goes in its own pull request, after a sweep of the tests that run the binary with this repository as the working directory.

payload.alternatives: Only the gate rejudging from the chain: it leaves a move written by hand with a valid key, which both readers would still pass. Only the readers judging: the product would still write, signed, a move its own readers refuse. Only saying so on the page: no gap would close.
payload.rationale: A move of a decision, a task, a skill or a run is judged against the chain, not a cache. First, under the lock, the gate reads the subject's state from the chain itself (a byte scan of the segments by id, to be measured), so a tampered projection can no longer let an illegal move be written. Then the state machine enters the format and both readers, the TypeScript verify and the Python reader, judge each transition at its position: an illegal move, or one whose from is not the state its writer saw, is not applied and is named in the census, with the verdict and exit unchanged. A run ends once; a move to a successor that does not exist, or of a subject never born, is illegal. Refusing on it is a later, separate choice.
payload.title: Hold every workflow move to its state machine, at the write and at every reader

payload.alternatives: No promise while the version is 0.x: someone who upgrades one clone and not another loses the record without knowing why. Skipping the kinds a reader does not know: an older verify would pass facts it cannot judge, against the proof the product sells.
payload.rationale: From the first version on npm, the format promises two things, written in FORMAT.md section 4.1 and held by a test. Every newer binary reads every older record, as the upcasters already do. An older binary that meets a kind or a field it does not know refuses, and says which version reads that record, instead of reading it wrong. A verify never says VERIFIED about facts its reader cannot judge. The order between tails, which is the writer's clock, stays a declared limit, outside the promise.
payload.title: Promise backward reading and a named refusal forward, from the first publication

payload.alternatives: 0.3.0: it reads as the continuation of the withdrawn pre-releases. 0.2.0: almost the number of a withdrawn pre-release with other content. A pre-release on a next dist-tag: friction for whoever arrives, and what a plain install picks would need measuring first.
payload.rationale: What reaches npm is a new concept and starts its own line at 0.1.0: it does not continue the withdrawn GitHub pre-releases nor the 0.x alpha. The five public packages (chain, core, context, stacks, code) publish together at that version; the action, the SDK and the VS Code extension keep running from a checkout. The tag v0.1.0 is born on the commit that is published, and a GitHub release, if any, carries only notes that point at npm, since provenance proves where the packages came from. The changelog presents 0.2.0-beta and 0.1.0-beta as withdrawn pre-releases from before this line.
payload.title: Publish the first npm version as 0.1.0, the start of a new line

payload.alternatives: Repositioning now as governance of any automation: the first README would promise what no prototype holds. Keeping the three lines with no track at all: the headless pieces that exist would stay unnamed.
payload.rationale: The first publication presents mnema as the record of the decisions behind coding agents' work, and keeps the three lines of where-it-fits: not an agent runner, not a copy somewhere else, not access control. The headless mode that already exists and is tested (an agent's own key, the CI recipe) is shown as a satellite of the core. Governing other automations is an exploratory track, kept off the README until a prototype exists, in this order: a rule whose target is a named action and not only a path, then a headless example with the SDK, an agent key and a run, and only then a server. The field reading, 6 of 9,448 tool calls to the server, says the value arrives through the host's hook, so a central API nobody intercepts for would not be asked.
payload.title: Launch as the decision record for coding agents, with headless CI as a satellite

payload.alternatives: Keeping it among the core's features: the front page would keep mixing a separate line of product into the central promise. Splitting the stack commands into a binary of their own: a large change that proves nothing more.
payload.rationale: Stacks installs skills and agents that others publish, with a signed adoption. It is the product farthest from the core promise, which is the decisions that govern the work, so the front page shows it as a satellite in the mnema family, with its own status, and no longer inside the core's features. Only the presentation changes: it stays the published package @mnema/stacks, and the stack commands stay in mnema.
payload.title: Show Stacks as a satellite of the core, not as part of its promise

payload.alternatives: Taking all seven off the table: it would drop Qwen Code, the one of them that a job without an account can hold. Changing nothing: the Antigravity note would keep contradicting its documentation.
payload.rationale: The seven hosts that sit on the lowest rung by their documentation were each read again at their sources. Before the first publication, Continue (whose project has closed and whose repository is read-only) and Warp (whose hooks are only a draft) leave the table for the line that covers any MCP client, and the note on Antigravity, which says it has no SessionStart while its documentation shows one, is corrected in the same change. After the publication, Qwen Code is ported with its own contract and a CI job that needs no account, since it turns a Claude Code plugin into an extension that loads its hooks. Cursor's editor, Antigravity, Factory Droid and Goose stay on the lowest rung and climb only by a capture made by hand.
payload.title: Take Continue and Warp off the host table, and port Qwen Code after the first publication

payload.alternatives: An opt-in core profile: two surfaces to test before there is evidence it is needed. Merging the five audit tools into one: breaks tool names for a saving not yet measured. Moving the audit tools to the command line only: takes the tool from an agent that audits, on a sample of zero.
payload.rationale: No tool of the MCP server is cut, merged or renamed before the first publication. A tool's name is a contract (the hooks, the skills and every hand-made configuration call it by name), and the only sample of use is 12 calls, all from tests, which convicts no tool. After the publication a local count of calls per tool, kept outside the record and with no change to the format, gives real use before any cut. The cost stays where it is measured: the 27 definitions weigh 54,568 bytes in the hosts that send them all.
payload.title: Keep the 27 tools as they are until their use is measured

If the npm organization can trust the repository's workflow for packages that do not exist yet, the first publication goes through that OIDC trust. If it cannot, a granular token limited to publishing in the @mnema scope, with a short life, is kept as a repository secret for that one run and revoked right after it, and the trusted publisher is configured for every later version. Once it is, the packages require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens, as npm advises.

payload.alternatives: Leaving both as declared debt: the guard's protected-key path would stay unheld, and a changed description would keep costing a red CI run.
payload.rationale: Two tests the suite lacks. The guard answers the refusal this machine's key would give, but its paired tests tie the person's protected key only with no passphrase set, so a guard that refused every protected key even with the passphrase present would pass them all: a fourth paired test covers that side. And a change to a tool's description must move the four weights the host contracts pin, which the local suite skips, so a local test now fails when a description changes without them, before CI does. A machine with no key at all keeps answering MISSING_WHO, as decided earlier.
payload.title: Hold the guard's key check with a passphrase set, and catch a changed tool description locally

payload.alternatives: Refusing only the title of spaces: punctuation alone would still pass as a title. Accepting both as today: a record could hold tasks no one can tell apart.
payload.rationale: A title made only of spaces, or only of punctuation, says nothing about the work, so it is refused with a code by the same rule at the command line and in the MCP tools that take a title, instead of being recorded as if it named something. It changes what a tool accepts, and lands after the first publication.
payload.title: Refuse a title with no content, at every door

payload.alternatives: Running them before the first publication: model cost and time on the critical path, for a number the launch does not need. Declaring and dropping them: the questions that decide whether the record changes an agent's work would stay unasked.
payload.rationale: No published result compares a superseded decision in the record with the same rule in a CLAUDE.md, and the page that says how each claim is held must not let a reader assume one: a line says it has no result. The experiments that need a paid model (the proof of the token cuts through the plugin's eval, capture without a person asking, the superseded decision against CLAUDE.md) run after the first publication, with a budget the maintainer sets at the time; nothing runs a paid model without that order.
payload.title: Say on the evidence page that the comparison with CLAUDE.md has no result yet, and run the model experiments after the first publication

payload.alternatives: Building it before the first publication: a design with no independent interview and no measurement. Dropping it: recording would stay entirely manual, which is where the record and the practice part ways.
payload.rationale: Capture redesigned from the commit (the commit or the pull request is the source, the agent proposes the decision and it stays private until accepted, with a hook on the shell) stays off the path to the first publication. It comes back with interviews of people other than the maintainer, of whom there are none yet, and with a measurement that needs a paid model.
payload.title: Build capture from the commit after the first publication, on real interviews and a measurement

payload.alternatives: Building it before the first publication, with the CI case still open: a silent loss. Dropping it: a refusal stays only a refusal, with no way to approve it later.
payload.rationale: A write the record refuses could become a request kept outside the record that a person signs later. Before any of it is built, a study of who sees that queue and of what happens in a CI run with no person: there, a request would be lost in silence. It comes after the first publication. A signed inbox stays turned down, as its study advised.
payload.title: Study who sees a deferred write before building the queue, after the first publication

payload.alternatives: Leaving it for after the first publication: it would then change as a format change under the compatibility promise, with older binaries refusing records they read today.
payload.rationale: What a reader accepts is part of the format the first publication freezes. A stored line that differs from its canonical bytes only by whitespace, or by a composed against a decomposed form of the same characters, is read today without a rule written down. The rule (refuse the non-canonical line, or read it and name it) is designed together with the control characters a reader shows, in the same pass, and decided before the format's compatibility promise takes effect.
payload.title: Settle what both readers do with a stored line that differs from the canonical one only by space or Unicode composition, before the format is frozen

payload.alternatives: Adding it before the first publication: more identity surface to explain and hold before launch. Dropping it for good: closes a door no measurement has yet asked to close.
payload.rationale: Sigstore already countersigns a checkpoint as a witness. Using it also to say who signs a fact, beside the key, adds identity surface (an e-mail address, or a repository, workflow and run, in a public log) and touches nothing the record proves today, so it waits until after the first publication.
payload.title: Keep Sigstore a witness, and leave it as a second way of naming the signer until after the first publication

payload.alternatives: Waiting for a pilot before any study: a need the format has to meet would surface after the freeze, as a format change under the compatibility promise. Planning to build it after the publication without a pilot: design for a need no user has stated.
payload.rationale: The first publication carries what is ready today. The organization layer, many repositories of one organization read together, is studied now, read-only and bounded to three questions: what the format must allow before it is frozen, so that the layer does not become a format change later; what a pilot would measure; and how it keeps the line that mnema is not a copy somewhere else, with a remote that never writes. Nothing of it is built before a pilot, and the pilot starts only after the publication, with the published product.
payload.title: Launch what is ready, study the organization layer now, and start its pilot only after the first publication

payload.alternatives: All four after the first publication: the paths the format freeze rests on would ship with their tests unmeasured. Retiring the old roadmap: drops mutation testing, the one block that measures whether the tests hold.
payload.rationale: Of the blocks the roadmap of August 2026 left open, mutation testing serves the proof of what is about to be published, so it runs before the first publication on the core paths, as part of hardening the record. Attestation already comes with the provenance of the first publication. The generated differential and conformance suite, the final page and the plugin's evals come after it; the front page is reworked before it as its own step.
payload.title: Run mutation testing on what is published before the first publication, and leave the other blocks of the old roadmap for after

A blank line between lines is declared in FORMAT.md, and both readers keep skipping it. On screen, every character that draws nothing is escaped, the whole class as a fixed list from Unicode 17, held by a test that turns red when one is missed.

A pointer from a repository to its organization's rules stays out of the signed record until a pilot asks for it. Who states an organization's rule is whoever writes in that organization's repository, since mnema is not access control. The pilot runs after the first publication, on an organization with at least three repositories that the maintainer names then, and nothing of the layer is built before it.

payload.alternatives: (b) Answer `ask`: a person gets a way through in Claude Code, VS Code and Copilot CLI, but Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and OpenCode do not hold a write for a person on `ask` (Codex rejects it, Cursor ignores it, and the doors for Gemini CLI and OpenCode never send it), so there it would let the write through. One answer would mean different things per host. (c) Keep letting the write through: the refusal would stop holding exactly when nobody can tell which rules apply, and the older machines of a mixed team would lose their refusals in silence. (d) Skip the line in the gate only: the skipped line may be the one that creates or retracts the rule, so the gate would decide wrongly both ways; it breaks "never skipped" and needs a tolerant reader the format refuses. Refuse only for the public tree: the private and global trees hold rules and switches that apply too, so letting the write through there is (c) for two trees of three, while which tree holds the line is a fact the text can say.
payload.rationale:
Context. The per-edit gate (the command hook `mnema before-a-write` and the MCP route `rules_before_an_edit`) decides a refusal by reading the record. A stored line the reader refuses (not JSON, a kind or field this version does not know, as a newer mnema's line is, or non-canonical bytes) makes that reading throw. The gate then answered nothing: the command exited 1 with an empty reply, which the plugin's wrappers turn into silence (so Copilot CLI, which denies on a non-zero exit, never sees it), and the MCP route answered a tool error, on which Claude Code's mcp_tool hook does not block (measured on 2.1.281). In every host the plugin wires, the write went through. The format says such a line is never guessed at and never skipped (FORMAT §7.1; the decision "Promise backward reading and a named refusal forward, from the first publication"). The gate reads three trees: the project's public tree (committed), the project's private tree and the machine-global tree (neither versioned). The global tree is read by every project on the machine.

Decision. When the reading throws an unreadable stored line, and only then, both doors answer deny. The command exits 0 and answers in each host's shape; the MCP route answers with a reply, not a tool error. Nothing is recorded, and a note goes to the second stream. The reason is fixed text around the reader's own refusal. It names the tree (the project's public record, the project's private record on this machine, or this machine's global record), gives the reader's own refusal with the file and position, and says how far the refusal reaches and the way out. The ways out: update mnema if a newer one wrote the line; for the public tree, restore the line from the repository's history; for the private and global trees, which are not versioned, restore the file from a copy or repair or remove the line. For the global tree the text says that every project on the machine is closed. A busy tail or a fault of the product is not turned into a refusal, and a torn last line is still dropped. In an MCP session over a workspace of several projects, an unreadable line in another project also refuses, and the text says "the project".

Consequences. An older mnema that meets a line a newer one wrote refuses every write in the project, or in every project on the machine when the line is in the global tree, until it is updated or the line is restored. There is no way out through the switch: `mnema switch off edit-refuses-a-write` reads the same record and is refused too. With no `mnema` on the PATH, or a hook that times out or fails for another reason, the gate still lets the write through. These refusals record no fact, because a refusal fact cites a rule and none could be read. The rule the plugin's handlers are written to follow, that a session is never made worse than without the plugin, has one exception, declared in docs/features.md and in the CHANGELOG: a record that cannot be read closes the writes.
payload.title: A gate that cannot read the record refuses the write

fields.note: Accepted: a gate that cannot read the record must refuse the write, in all three trees.

payload.alternatives: (A) Refuse every committed key without a tail: every machine and every agent enrolled before its first write would fail, and in a one-tail record deleting the keys with the tail would still read as a record with no events and pass. (B) Make the second reader say what the product says: the readers would agree, on "verified" over a record with no event left in it. (D) Pin the divergence as it stands: it pins exit 0 against exit 3 on the same bytes, and the second reader would still answer differently depending on whether a tail's proof survived. (E) A new exit code for the empty record: a script can let that code through, and both readers already give one exit for "what was asked for is not here". Refusing only where a committed key remains: deleting the keys too would bring the exit back to 0.
payload.rationale:
Context. A key's fingerprint is the id of the tail it writes, so a record's committed keys are a roster of the tails that should exist (FORMAT section 6.5), and a committed key with no tail is said as a note, never as a refusal, because an absence is not something a reader can prove was tampering. Section 6.5 does not say what a reader answers when no tail is left at all: the tails/ directory gone, no tail directory in it, or only tails that hold no event and no checkpoint, which section 4 does not count. There the two readers part on the same bytes. On a record of one tail (14 events, 7 checkpoints, a person's key and a declared backup) with its tail directory deleted, `mnema verify` says "verified (T1 only); 0 tail(s); no events yet", with a census note for each key, and exits 0; the second reader says BROKEN ("there are no tails", or "there is no tails/ directory" when that is gone), exits 3 and never reaches its section 6.5 notes. With the tail directory kept and only its tail proof left in it, the second reader says VERIFIED and exits 0. With every public key deleted as well, the product still exits 0. Under `--require signed` the product exits 1 on all of these, because no event is signature-covered. A record does not reach this shape through `mnema init` when it succeeds: init writes three events and a checkpoint before it returns. It does reach it when init fails after making the directory (measured with a home it cannot write to): `.mnema/` is left with its `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes`, and a second `mnema init` answers "nothing to found" and writes nothing. The compatibility promise starts at the first publication, which has not happened, and it forbids loosening a rule, not tightening one (FORMAT section 7.1).

Decision. A record in which no tail holds an event or a checkpoint asserts no fact, and both readers refuse it by name, at every value of `--require`, with the exit of any other refusal (1), not a new one. FORMAT section 4 says so beside the rule that an empty tail is not counted, and section 6.5 says that its notes still run there, so each committed key with no tail is still named. The product applies the rule to the committed tree always, and to the private and global trees only when they hold a record (a key or a tail), as it already decides today which of those trees it rules on. The second reader turns its two early stops (no tails/ directory, no tail directory in it) into that refusal under section 4, and keeps BROKEN for a path with no directory at it. A committed key with no tail beside a tail that holds events stays a note, as it is now.

Consequences. A checkout with no tail holding anything fails `mnema verify` by default instead of passing it: tails removed by a merge, left out by a sparse checkout, or deleted in a commit, also when that commit is older than the revision `--since` compares with; so does a record erased with its keys and its `.mnema/.gitignore` left. A `.mnema/` that holds no tail because `mnema init` failed half way, or because it was made by hand and every write went to the private tree, fails until a first write to the public tree founds it; running `init` again does not. In `verify --workspace`, such a project is refused, and `--allow-no-record` does not excuse it, since the project is there. The surfaces that show this verdict (the SDK's verify, the VS Code status bar) show the refusal. The Action already failed these records when the pull request removes the tails, through `--require signed` and `--since`, and its comment now quotes the reason by name; a repository where neither the base nor the head holds a segment is still reported by the Action as holding no record, and passes, as before. The text that today calls a record with no tail "indistinguishable from a fresh one" is corrected, because a fresh record holds the founding. What stays open, and stays said in the docs and in `--json`: one tail removed whole while another remains (both readers verify it, `--require signed` included), the newest events cut together with their checkpoint, a record erased and founded again, and a removal of that first kind committed before the revision `--since` compares with. Only a copy of the record from before (`--since <rev>`, a git remote) shows those. The external witness dates a checkpoint and keeps no copy, so it does not.
payload.title: A record in which no tail holds anything is refused by both readers, by name

fields.note: Accepted: a record with no tail holding anything asserts no fact, so both readers refuse it by name.

payload.alternatives: A short-lived token kept as a repository secret for the first run: a stored publishing credential for a single use, which the maintainer prefers not to create. Waiting for npm to allow trusted publishing of a package that does not exist yet: it blocks the first publication on a change nobody has announced.
payload.rationale: npm's trusted publishing can only be configured for a package that already exists, so the first version of the five packages is published by the maintainer from a terminal, logged in with two-factor authentication, from the tarballs packed at the commit the version names, in the order chain, core, context, stacks, code. That first version carries no provenance, since provenance is made only in CI. Right after it, a trusted publisher is configured for each of the five packages, pointing at this repository's release workflow, and every later version is published by CI through OIDC, with provenance and no stored token; the packages then require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens, as npm advises.
payload.title: Publish the first version by hand, then let CI publish every later one through npm's trusted publishing

payload.alternatives: Changesets: it versions only the package.json files, so the other ten places would need the same script, and it writes a changelog per package that competes with the curated one. release-please or semantic-release: both read Conventional Commit prefixes, and semantic-release publishes on every merge with no person approving.
payload.rationale: The version is one number held in nineteen places: nine package.json files, seven plugin manifests, the version constant, the help golden and the console recording. A script in the repository, run as pnpm release:prepare, proposes the next number from the changelog's Unreleased section (Added, Changed or Removed raise the minor while the line is 0.x, Fixed alone raises the patch, and a number can be given instead), writes it in every one of those places through the same finders the version guard uses, regenerates the golden and the recording, and cuts the changelog; the result is an ordinary pull request named Release x.y.z, reviewed and held by CI. When it merges, a release workflow builds, packs the five public packages and publishes them through npm's trusted publishing with provenance, waiting in a GitHub environment whose required reviewer is the maintainer; only after the publication does it create the tag vx.y.z and a GitHub release whose notes are that changelog section with a link to npm and no tarballs. No package.json, tag or release is edited by hand, the single hand-written changelog stays, and commit titles keep their style.
payload.title: Version and release the packages by a script and a release workflow the maintainer approves

A local count of tool calls comes with it. The experiments that need a paid model wait for what the pilot shows matters.

payload.alternatives: Only printing the line to add, without touching the file: the person or agent that runs `init` is the one that would have to act, and the pilot showed they act by hand only after being burned. Warning in `verify` once the tailproof is already reformatted: catches the damage after it is done. Touching no file outside `.mnema/` at all: leaves the record exposed in every repository with prettier, which in the pilot was every repository.
payload.rationale: In the first real-use pilot both agents had to add `.mnema/` to `.prettierignore` by hand, because prettier and lint-staged would rewrite `tailproof.json` and break the signatures; and one agent read an instruction about the folder as "commit it as it is" and recorded nothing. So `init` creates `.mnema/README.md` (what the folder is, that it changes with the work and goes in the same commit as the work it describes, that nothing in it is edited or reformatted, that private keys are never in it, how to verify it), and, when the repository declares prettier (a `.prettierignore`, `prettier` in the root package.json, or a `.prettierrc*`), adds `.mnema/` to `.prettierignore` and says so. Running `init` again on a project that already has `.mnema/` adds only what is missing; `mnema doctor` points at both gaps. The README is outside the proof, like `.gitignore`, and both readers accept it.
payload.title: mnema init writes a README into .mnema/ and keeps a declared formatter off the record

payload.alternatives: Also adding `.mnema/` to `.prettierignore` on the first write: zero friction, but the product would edit a file of the person's without anyone asking. Leaving existing projects to a manual `mnema init`: every project recorded before the upgrade would stay without the README and unprotected until someone thought of it. Creating the README on any connection, reads included: breaks the promise that a read changes nothing.
payload.rationale: Upgrading mnema should not require remembering a command for every existing project. The README lives inside `.mnema/`, where every write already lands and which is committed with the work, so the first signed write in a project whose public record has no README creates it alongside, and the write's result says so. A read never creates it and a refused write never creates it: a connection that only reads leaves the repository as it found it, and a refusal leaves nothing. The repository's own `.prettierignore` is the person's file, so nothing edits it automatically: the session brief says, in one line, that a declared formatter can rewrite the record and that `mnema init` protects it.
payload.title: A project initialized before the README gets it with its first signed write; only init edits .prettierignore

payload.alternatives: A cache the writer keeps of whether rules exist: goes stale the moment a rule arrives by git pull or checkout without this machine writing anything, which is a false negative. Leaving the 200 ms: every edit in two hosts pays for a check that has nothing to check. Changing the Claude Code hook too: it already costs about 1 ms.
payload.rationale: Measured on 21 October 2026 (sandbox, 50 runs, 0.1.1): in Claude Code the edit hook is an MCP call to a server already up, about 1 ms per edit, so nothing changes there; in Cursor and VS Code it is a process per edit, about 200 ms even when the project has no rule with an address, about 70% of it loading mnema. The handler may decide without loading mnema that no tree (public, private, global) holds a link that addresses a path, by scanning the stored lines for the link's literal marker, and skip; anything else, including an unreadable tree or an unknown format, runs mnema. A false positive costs the 200 ms of today; a false negative would let a write through without the rule, which is the one thing the hook exists to prevent.
payload.title: The Cursor and VS Code edit hook may skip launching mnema only when no tree can hold an addressed rule, never on a cache

payload.alternatives: 0.2.0 because new commands and options arrive: semver would allow it in 0.x, but the maintainer judged that a minor so soon after the first publication reads as more change than there is. A release per pull request: several versions in days, each with its own approval in the npm environment.
payload.rationale: The work since 0.1.1 (the tag that waits for npm, the local tool-call count, the README and formatter protection, the automatic README, the held text debts, the scanners and the guard mutation, the refused inputs, the Cursor and VS Code hook shortcut) is small, changes no format, and can be reviewed one pull request at a time; releasing each piece separately would be several versions in a few days. It stays a patch version, 0.1.2, as the maintainer chose: the first minor after 0.1.0 is kept for a step the users would notice as one.
payload.title: Batch the small ready work into 0.1.2 instead of releasing it a little at a time

payload.text: Run on 20 and 21 October 2026 in safeaccess-inline and safeaccess-identum, one new Claude Code session per repository with the mnema 0.1.1 plugin, resolving their 13 Dependabot pull requests and three policy decisions each; the prompt never asked to record. Inline: 0 of 3 decisions recorded unasked; the agent said it did not record because the prompt asked to commit `.mnema/` as it was. Identum, with that phrase removed: 3 of 3 recorded unasked, each in the commit that implements it, plus one `record_observation` correcting the premise of one of them from the Dependabot log. `capture_memory` was used 0 times in both: what the agents learnt went to the host's own memory. Both agents protected `.mnema/` from prettier by hand. The edit hook ran on every edit (23) and found no addressed rule each time. Both records are committed and verified by the Python reader.

payload.alternatives: The maintainer accepting every decision with his own key: the strongest proof of assent, but in practice it was double work on decisions already his, and the cost falls on exactly the decisions that need it least. The agent accepting everything it records: loses the line between what the maintainer chose and what the agent concluded, which is the line a later reader most needs.
payload.rationale: On 21 October 2026 the maintainer ran `mnema decision move accept` five times in a day, across three repositories, copying 36-character ids, each time for a decision he had himself just chosen in the conversation: the acceptance added friction and no judgement. The switch `agent-accepts` is on in this repository, and an acceptance made through the MCP is recorded as the agent's and marked so wherever it is read, so the record stays honest about who acted. So when the maintainer dictates a decision (answers the question that settles it), the agent records it and accepts it at once, with a note that quotes his answer. A decision the agent proposes on its own judgement still waits for the maintainer's own `accept`, signed with his key.
payload.title: The agent accepts the decisions the maintainer dictated in the session; what the agent proposes alone waits for the maintainer

fields.note: Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026, answering how to reduce the friction of accepting: "Eu aceito o que você ditou".

payload.alternatives: notagrafo as the second repository: an AGENTS.md generated by the old alpha would confound what the agent reads. Refining the study before the pilot: the research and the choices it forces are the part that tests recording, so doing it outside the pilot removes the material. Implementing the first phase in the same session: a much larger session whose code would dominate what is measured.
payload.rationale: The first pilot measured agents on CI policy and dependency updates in two repositories of one family. monitor-sefaz differs on every axis the first round left open: another stack (pnpm and turbo, an app), Portuguese, no commitlint, a declared prettier (the first test of the 0.1.2 init protection), an empty AGENTS.md, and above all a product study whose outcome is a set of scope decisions with real alternatives (which fiscal documents enter a first phase, whether the panel's model becomes document, state, authorizer, environment and service, what to do with NFS-e). That is the kind of decision mnema exists to keep. The session resolves the open Dependabot pull requests, refines the coverage study against primary sources and the code, and stops at the scope decisions; implementing new documents waits for an accepted study. It runs after 0.1.2 so the local tool-call count is measured for the first time. The study stays out of git, as the maintainer chose.
payload.title: Run the second real-use pilot on monitor-sefaz after 0.1.2, with product decisions as the work

fields.note: Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026: monitor-sefaz after 0.1.2; the pilot session refines the study ("A sessão do piloto"); the study stays out of git ("Fora do git"); scope is the bot PRs, the study and the decisions.

payload.alternatives: Having init also edit each of those tools' configuration, as it does `.prettierignore`: less friction, but it would edit YAML and JSON-with-comments configuration files of several tools whose formats change between versions, on the person's behalf. Covering only prettier: leaves the record exposed to the next tool, which the first pilot showed is found only after the damage. Only the verify diagnosis: catches every tool but always after the bytes changed.
payload.rationale: Prettier is the most common of a class: tools that rewrite files nobody looks at. EditorConfig-aware editors add a final newline, trim trailing space or change line ends on save; the pre-commit framework's end-of-file-fixer, trailing-whitespace, mixed-line-ending and pretty-format-json hooks rewrite at commit; Biome and dprint format JSON without reading .prettierignore; lint-staged can run any of them on staged `.mnema/` files. Any of these breaks the signatures. So: `init` (and the first write, as with the README) writes `.mnema/.editorconfig` that unsets the parent's rules, inside the record's own folder like `.gitattributes`, touching no file of the person's; `doctor` and the session brief detect a pre-commit config, Biome, dprint or lint-staged that reaches `.mnema/` and say the line to add to each, editing nothing; and `verify`, when a stored line differs from its canonical form only by space, line end or formatting, says a formatter rewrote it and how to restore it, instead of only failing. What a reader accepts does not change.
payload.title: Guard the record against the other tools that rewrite files: an .editorconfig inside .mnema/, warnings for the rest, and a verify that names a reformat

fields.note: Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026, choosing for 0.1.2: ".editorconfig dentro do .mnema/", "O verify diagnostica" and "doctor/brief avisam das outras"; not having init edit the other tools' configuration.

payload.alternatives: Leaving it to the release notes: the person who updates one half never reads them at the moment the hook goes quiet. Having the plugin refuse to run with a mismatched binary: turns a silent degradation into a hard stop for the agent, where a line that names the fix is enough. Bundling the binary inside the plugin: two copies of mnema on one machine, with the identity and key questions that brings.
payload.rationale: A newer plugin with an older binary leaves the edit hook silent: the binary refuses a flag the plugin passes and nothing reaches the person or the agent. Upgrading to 0.1.2 makes this likely, because the binary (npm) and the plugin (the host's plugin manager) are updated separately. So the hook says in one line, on the channel the host shows, that the two do not match and which `npm i -g @mnema/code@<version>` brings the binary level, without blocking the agent's write; the session brief says the same when it detects it; and `mnema doctor` compares the installed plugin's version with the binary on the PATH. The compatibility rule comes from what the plugin actually passes to the binary: an older binary is the case that breaks.
payload.title: When the plugin and the binary disagree on version, the hook, the brief and doctor say so with the command that fixes it

payload.alternatives: Checking docs links on every pull request: a pull request would fail for a third-party site being down. Relying on Dependabot alerts alone for advisories: they cover what GitHub's database maps to the manifest; osv-scanner reads the lockfile and other sources, and it is already in CI.
payload.rationale: The post-merge link job checks only the READMEs' external links, so a link in docs/ can rot unnoticed; and the advisory scan runs only on pull requests and pushes, so a new advisory against an unchanged lockfile waits for the next dependency change. Both gaps were found when the scanners entered CI on 21 October 2026. The link job extends to docs/ with the care it already has (after the merge, never blocking a pull request on the network), and osv-scanner gains a weekly schedule.
payload.title: Check the external links of docs/ after each merge and run the dependency advisory scan weekly

payload.text: The review of the first implementation (21 October 2026) found that prettier declared only in the package.json of a monorepo subproject, where `mnema init` ran, is not detected: the detection reads only the git root. The maintainer chose to have it read the mnema project's own directory as well, and to write `.prettierignore` where prettier reads it. It ships with the guard against the other formatters (ADR-32).
payload.topic: The formatter detection also reads the project's own directory

fields.note: Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026, choosing for 0.1.2: "Plugin × binário desencontrados".
Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026, choosing for 0.1.2: "Os furos de CI".

payload.alternatives: Treating mnema as the replacement for the person's own notes and asking them to move: the pilot showed people and agents keep their channel by habit, and a record that exists only when the habit breaks is empty. Avoiding duplication by recording only what no other channel holds: makes mnema the leftover, and a decision that lives only in a ledger or a host's memory is neither signed nor verifiable nor shared with the clone. Relying on the instructions alone ("record as the work happens"): the pilot and the planning session both had them and still did not record.
payload.rationale: The first real-use pilot and the maintainer's own planning session showed one pattern three times: mnema loses whenever a richer channel already exists. The inline agent kept what it learnt in the host's memory and recorded nothing; the planning session wrote its decisions into its own bench (handoffs, the alignment file) and recorded them only when asked, twice in one day; the identum agent recorded 3 of 3 because it had nowhere else to put them. A user will almost always have such a channel: a plan, a ledger, an ADR folder, CLAUDE.md, the host's memory. So the product does not ask the person to give it up and does not wait for it to be absent: mnema takes part in the work beside it, at the moments the work already passes through (a choice settled in a question, a note written to the host's memory, a plan or decision file written, a handoff to another agent), and is read back where the work reads, so recording pays for itself in the same session. Duplication with the person's own notes is accepted: the record is the signed, append-only, verifiable copy, which the others are not. This holds for every host and every surface mnema covers, each through the channel that host offers.
payload.title: mnema is always in the equation: it records alongside the person's own notes, ledgers and the host's memory, even when that duplicates them, in every host

fields.note: Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026: "mesmo que o usuario ja tenha uma bancada dele ... o mnema tem que sempre entrar nessa equação, sempre deve ser o centro mesmo que duplique ... isso para todo os host e coberturas".

payload.alternatives: The two cheapest Claude Code hooks in 0.1.2 and the rest later: covers one host and leaves the principle half-applied in the release that introduces it. A separate 0.1.3 round before the second pilot: keeps 0.1.2 on time, but the maintainer judged a short delay worth a complete release.
payload.rationale: The maintainer chose to ship ADR-35 whole in 0.1.2 rather than split it into a later round: a release that measures and fixes how agents use mnema (the pilot findings, the init, the hooks) would be incomplete without the part that makes mnema present at the moments the work passes through. The front covers, for every host mnema supports and through the channel each one offers: the moment a choice is settled (a hook after the question tool in Claude Code, a reading of the turn at Stop where there is no such tool) proposing `record_decision`; the host's own memory mirrored into `capture_memory`, duplicating on purpose; a plan, ledger, ADR, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md written with decision-shaped content proposing to record alongside; one sentence in the server instructions saying to record here even when notes are kept elsewhere; and briefs and handoffs that cite and read the record back. It starts with a map of host by moment by channel. The release may slip for it.
payload.title: 0.1.2 carries the presence front complete, in every host, even if the release slips

payload.text: On 21 October 2026, choosing the presence mechanisms, the maintainer went further: mnema should be the center of everything for the user, all the time, for everything and for everyone ("o mnema deve ser o centro de tudo para o usuario, deve ser tudo que o mnema precisa o tempo todo para tudo e para todos"). The presence study is to take this as its north: every moment a person or an agent decides, learns, plans, hands over or asks why, on every host and surface (MCP, CLI, hooks, the CI Action, the VS Code extension, the SDK), and say what mnema does at each.

fields.note: Dictated by the maintainer on 21 October 2026: "Temos que incluir tudo para entrar para o 0.1.2 já de forma completa, pode atrasar o 0.1.2 um pouco não tem problema", with all four mechanisms chosen.

payload.alternatives: Recording a proposed decision on its own after every answered question: it would read the person's words into the record by default, and the existing reading of corrections starts off for that reason. Only suggesting `capture_memory` when the host's memory is written: the pilot showed it used 0 times in 2 sessions. Mirroring the host's memory into the public record: that memory is private to the machine. Adding a hook-only MCP tool: grows the 27 definitions every session pays for. Asking for one more turn at Stop: an extra model turn after every reply.
payload.rationale: Applies ADR-35 and ADR-36 from the presence study of 21 October 2026, which mapped every supported host by moment and channel. After a question to the person is answered (Claude Code `AskUserQuestion`, Copilot `ask_user`, Codex `request_user_input`, Gemini `ask_user`, OpenCode `question`), a post-tool hook adds one factual sentence to the agent's context that the choice is not in the record and `record_decision` keeps it; it records nothing, so it is on by default under a switch of its own. A note the agent writes into the host's own memory directory is mirrored, deterministically and without asking the agent, into this machine's private tree as a memory, deduplicated by a content hash, leaving out the host's index and the notes about the person; whether this mirror is on by default is left to the maintainer. A plan, ledger, ADR or instructions file written with decision-shaped content gets one line naming the command that records or imports it, once per file per session, and nothing is written to the public record by it. The server instructions gain the sentence to record here even what is kept elsewhere, within the 2,048-character ceiling by two measured cuts. A subagent receives the session brief when it starts. Hosts whose channel is documented but not measured are wired and labelled as not measured.
payload.title: How mnema is present at the moments of the work in 0.1.2: a fact after a settled question, the host's memory mirrored privately, a line beside decision files, and the instructions and subagents

payload.content: A defect of the core found on 21 October 2026 while reviewing the Cursor and VS Code hook shortcut: in a linked git worktree whose `.git` file has a `gitdir:` that passes through a symlink and whose `commondir` is relative, mnema resolves the common dir textually over the symlinked path and reads the private tree at a place that is not the real common dir (the reviewer's scenario 8: it read `$B/mnema/...`). The shortcut covers it by reading both spellings, but the core itself should resolve `commondir` against the real gitdir. Not fixed yet.

payload.text: The adversarial review of the first implementation (21 October 2026) showed that comparing a stored line only with its own canonical form lets a tampering pass as a reformat: change a value, add one space, and both readers said "a formatter or an editor did this", while the TypeScript reader's single issue hid the hash that no longer matched. The diagnosis is therefore said only when the canonical form recomputed from the reformatted line matches what was signed (the entry's chained hash; the signature of a checkpoint or tail proof), and a hash or signature mismatch is always reported beside it. What a reader accepts does not change; only which reason it gives.
payload.topic: The formatter diagnosis must be conditioned on the proof

payload.content: A reader disagreement found on 21 October 2026 by an adversarial review: the Python reader accepts (VERIFIED) a tail proof signed by ANOTHER key registered in the same project, while the TypeScript reader refuses it (bad-signature). `_signature_holds` in `packages/chain/verifier/mnemaverify/record.py` looks the key up by the proof's own `signerFp` instead of by the fingerprint the tail's id names, which is what `verifyTailOwnership` in the TypeScript reader uses. The defect predates the 0.1.2 round. Also pre-existing: when the TypeScript reader refuses a line (unreadable, not canonical), the tail is marked unreadable and the chain-break, content-root and signature issues of the rest of that tail are not reported beside it.

Found on 21 October 2026 by the adversarial review of the tail-ownership fix, and left for the maintainer as a format decision: FORMAT §6 does not require a tail's checkpoints to be signed by the tail's own key. Events grafted into person A's tail, with hashes and a checkpoint recomputed and signed by ANY enrolled key (another key of the same identity, or even the checker key of another identity), verify in all six readers (TypeScript, Python, the browser site; before and after the fix). Authorship is not forged (each event stays attributed to its signer, §6.2 holds), but the ownership of a tail is proven only at its birth (the tail proof), not for what is appended later. Separately: a file in `keys/` whose name does not match its material and that nothing uses is REFUSED by the Python reader (§6) and VERIFIED by the TypeScript reader and the site, a verdict disagreement with no proof effect.

payload.text: Three adversarial reviews on 21 October 2026 blocked the verify diagnosis in turn: comparing a line with its own canonical form let a tampering pass as a reformat; confirming it with the line's own stored hash let a tampering that recomputed that hash pass; and re-reading a canonicalised copy of the whole record on disk, the design that closed both, made a read write through a symlink inside `.mnema/` into a file of the person's (and failed without a verdict when TMPDIR was missing or empty). The orchestrating session took the diagnosis out of the 0.1.2 pull request: the `.editorconfig` inside `.mnema/` and the warnings about pre-commit, Biome, dprint and lint-staged ship; the diagnosis comes back as its own design that reads the canonical form in memory and copies nothing to disk. Both readers stay exactly as they are until then.
payload.topic: The verify diagnosis is held back from 0.1.2
